notes: Only the baa needs a fatHa: the alif already makes the long aa, and the final t has no vowel (not bataata or bataatu).
also: bataatan = 'not at all', as in 'laa, bataatan!' (No, not at all!)

how: ism (name) + HaDirtik (polite 'you', to a woman): literally 'the name of your presence?'
notes: A statement said with a question's rising tone; the full Levantine question adds shuu (what): shuu ism HaDirtik?
flag: near-duplicate of the carded 'shuu ism HaDirtik?': the Levantine line had shu; the bare rising-tone question is the Egyptian scene's pattern

how: inti (you, to a woman) + min (from) + ish-shaam (Damascus)
notes: In Syria, ish-shaam means Damascus; it can also mean the whole Levant.
Her dialect says the article as il-, and the l blends into the sh: ish-shaam.
Formal Arabic: hal anti min dimashq?
flag: translit capital S reads as Saad in Parker's convention, but the letter is shiin: fix to 'inti min ish-shaam?'

meaning_core: And you? Where are you from?
how: w- (and) + inte (you, to a man) + min ween (from where)
notes: In her dialect 'you' is inte to a man and inti to a woman; the book spells both the same way.
ween is Levantine for 'where'. Formal Arabic: wa anta? min ayna anta?

how: ana (I) + min (from) + Halab (Aleppo); Arabic needs no word for 'am'.
notes: Same words in formal Arabic and in her Levantine dialect.
Syria's great city in the north.
Starts with the breathy H (Haa'), not a plain h.

how: al- (the) + shaam: the l of al- blends into the sh, so you say ash-shaam.
notes: Her parallel: Egyptians call Cairo maSr (Egypt), and Syrians call Damascus ish-shaam.
The name of her dialect, shaami (Levantine), comes from this word.
also: Damascus, the way Syrians often use it
flag: translit capital S reads as Saad in Parker's convention, but the letter is shiin: fix to 'ash-shaam'

notes: Formal Arabic says miSr: same letters, different first vowel.
Just as Syrians call Damascus ish-shaam, Egyptians call Cairo maSr.
also: Cairo, the way Egyptians often use it

notes: Named after Alexander the Great: iskandar is Arabic for Alexander.
Egypt's big port city on the Mediterranean coast.

how: ana (I) + min (from) + al-iskandariyya (Alexandria); Arabic needs no word for 'am'.
notes: The al- is part of the city's name, like al-qaahira (Cairo).
Starts with cayn, the tight throat sound, not a plain i.
The name means 'pillar' or 'support'.
The final aa is written with a dotless yaa shape (alif maqSuura), but it sounds like alif.
Same s-l-m core as salaam (peace) in as-salaamu calaykum.
flag: translit capital S reads as Saad in Parker's convention, but the letter is siin: fix to 'salmaa'

notes: The name means 'companion in evening conversation'.
flag: translit capital S reads as Saad in Parker's convention, but the letter is siin: fix to 'saamir'

notes: Borrowed from French/English 'beige': 'just transliteration to Arabic'.
The jiim here is said like the s in 'measure', so it matches the English word.
Handwriting: she starts a little above the line so the baa-yaa zigzag fits; the book starts on the line. 'Both works.'

how: kulliyyat (college of) + aT-Tibb (the medicine): kulliyya's -a is said -at before the next word, as in jaamicat.
notes: Tibb = medicine; a doctor is Tabiib, from the same T-b-b letters.
Say aT-Tibb: the l of al- blends into the T.

how: nimra (number) + tilifuun (phone) + -ak (your, to a man): nimra's -a is said -it before the next word.
notes: The tutor for the oral assessment speaks Levantine, so expect her to ask for your nimrit tilifuun.
Formal Arabic: raqm tilifuunak.

how: cand (at) + -u (him): her dialect's short form of cindahu.
notes: Formal Arabic: cindahu.
flag: Arabic has a kasra under the cayn (reads cindu) but the translit and the Levantine form are candu: drop the kasra or make it a fatHa

how: ustaadha (female professor) + cindii (I have) + su'aal (question)
notes: 'From this moment onward, if you have a question, you have to say' this in her class.
To a male teacher: ustaadh, cindii su'aal.
Say the dh as in 'this': us-taa-dha.

how: cindii (I have) + su'aal (question): literally 'at me, a question'.
notes: su'aal has a catch (hamza) in the middle: su-'aal.
In her class, open with ustaadha: ustaadha, cindii su'aal.

how: hal (yes/no question word) + cindaka (you have, to a man) + su'aal (question)
notes: To a woman: hal cindaki su'aal? She asks both forms on purpose.
Answer with a full sentence: laa, laysa cindii su'aal.

meaning_core: No, I don't have a question
how: laa (no) + laysa cindii (I don't have) + su'aal (question)
notes: Just 'laa' is 'not wrong, but it's not very respectful': give the full sentence.
laysa, not laa: cindii isn't a verb (it literally means 'at me').
laa shukran (no, thank you) is 'too polite' for this question.

how: laa (no) + shukran (thank you)
notes: The answer to her joke khudh dhubaab ('Take some flies!').
Not for 'Do you have a question?': she called it 'too polite' there.
Arabic 'have' isn't a verb: cindii = 'at me' = I have; cindahu = 'at him' = he has.
It takes the same endings as a noun: -ii, -ka, -ki, -hu, -haa.
Starts with the throaty cayn, not a hamza: don't say English 'end'. 'Exaggerate to remember.'

how: cinda (at) + -ka (you, to a man): literally 'at you'.
notes: To a woman: cindaki.
Keep the a before the ending: cindaka, cindaki, cindahu (not the u of kitaabuka).
Forgot the endings on a test? 'Go to a noun you know really well' (baab, ism, kitaab) and copy its endings.

how: cinda (at) + -hu (him): literally 'at him'.
notes: She has: cindahaa.
In her Levantine dialect: candu.

how: cinda (at) + -naa (us): literally 'at us'.
notes: The -naa (us, our) ending is ARAB 102 material; this course teaches the singular endings.

how: jaar (neighbor) + -ii (my)
notes: jaar sounds like English 'jar', but means neighbor.

how: jaar (neighbor) + -uka (your, to a man): the u before -ka is part of the ending.
notes: 'jaaruk works' too: the everyday short form.
To a woman: jaaruki.

how: jaar (neighbor) + -uhaa (her): the u before -haa is part of the ending.
notes: Ends in -a, but that's the -haa (her), not a feminine ending.
jaar is a male neighbor; a female neighbor is jaara.

how: baab (door) + -uki (your, to a woman): the u before -ki is part of the ending.
notes: To a man: baabuka.
baab is 'the easiest one' for practicing endings: baabii, baabuka, baabuki, baabuhu, baabuhaa.

how: dajaaj (chicken) + jadiid (new): noun first, then the adjective, the reverse of English.
notes: dajaaj has no -a ending, so the adjective stays masculine: jadiid.

how: dhubaab (flies) + jadiid (new): noun first, then the adjective.
notes: Her joke to make it stick: 'new flies' could be spy-drone flies used by intelligence services.

how: jaamica (university) + jadiida (new): jaamica is feminine, so the adjective gets the feminine -a too.
notes: jaamica jadiid (no -a) would be wrong.

how: taa' (the letter t) + marbuuTa (tied): a 'tied t', shaped like haa' with two dots on top.
notes: Most words ending in an -a sound are feminine, written with this letter; no -a usually means masculine.
Traps: kitaabuhaa ends in -a, but that's -haa (her); haadhaa ends in -a but is masculine.
Said -a at the end of a word, but -at when another word follows: jaamicat Liberty.
'Don't forget the glottal stop at the end': masaa'.
Good evening = masaa' al-khayr, built just like SabaaH al-khayr (good morning).
Her Levantine drops the final stop: masa.

how: khudh (take!, to a man) + dhubaab (flies)
notes: Her joke drill; the expected answer is laa shukran (No, thank you).
Culture: handing someone something with 'khudh' is rude; say tafaDDal. khudh is fine with family and kids.
The dh has a sukuun (no vowel): 'dh, not dhu'.
Writing: alif and dhaal never join the next letter, so khaa' starts a new piece and the final taa' stands alone.
Her drill: she says khudh (take!), you answer akhadhtu (I took).

how: akhadhtu (I took) + the grade: Arabic says 'I took A'.
akhadhtu (I took) + dhubaab (flies)

notes: Arabic has no 'it': everything is he (huwa) or she (hiya).
Writing: dhaal and waaw never join the next letter, so it breaks into three pieces: yadh + uu + b.

how: huwa (he, it) + yadhuub (melts)
notes: Her example: snow (ath-thalj) is masculine, so it's huwa yadhuub.

how: al- (the) + thalj (snow): the l of al- blends into the th, so you say ath-thalj.
notes: Masculine (no -a ending), so it takes huwa: huwa yadhuub, 'it melts'.

how: dajaaj (chicken) + yadhuub (melts): Arabic uses 'melts' for thawing too.
dhaat (same) + ad-dajaaj (the chicken): the l of al- blends into the d.
notes: dhaat sounds like English 'that', but means 'the same' (or 'self').

how: dhaat (same) + adh-dhubaab (the flies): the l of al- blends into the dh.
notes: dhaat + a noun with al- means 'the same': dhaat ad-dajaaj, the same chicken.

how: dhaat (self) + -ii (my)
notes: Understood, but not the usual way to say it; nafsii is more common.

how: nafs (self, soul) + -ii (my)
notes: dhaatii means the same but is less common.

how: anta (you, to a man) + bilaa (without) + adab (manners): 'you are without manners'.
notes: Her example of when to say it: to men who catcall women.
adab has two meanings: literature, and (in everyday Levantine) manners.

how: bi- (with) + laa (no): literally 'with no'.
notes: Goes right before a noun: bilaa adab (no manners), bilaa sabab (no reason).
Her three negatives: laa (with verbs), laysa (with nouns and pronouns), and bilaa (without).
She called it 'more shaami' (Levantine), but it's fine in formal Arabic too.
Her example: bilaa sabab, 'for no reason'.

how: bilaa (without) + sabab (reason): 'without a reason'.
notes: Not 'laa sabab': Arabic wants the bi- 'connection' here.

how: laa (not) + uHibb (I like, I love)
notes: uHibb is a verb, so it's negated with laa, not laysa.

how: laa (not) + uHibb (I like) + ad-dajaaj (the chicken): Arabic says 'the' for things in general.
notes: Say ad-dajaaj: the l of al- blends into the d.
laa, not laysa, because uHibb is a verb.

how: uHibb (I like) + ad-dajaaj (the chicken): Arabic says 'the' for things in general.
notes: Say ad-dajaaj: the l of al- blends into the d.

how: hal (yes/no question word) + tuHibb (you like, to a man) + ad-dajaaj (the chicken)
notes: To a woman: hal tuHibbiin ad-dajaaj?
Answer: nacam, uHibb ad-dajaaj, or laa, laa uHibb ad-dajaaj.

how: hal (yes/no question word) + tuHibbiin (you like, to a woman) + ad-dajaaj (the chicken)
notes: The -iin ending shows you're talking to a woman; to a man: hal tuHibb ad-dajaaj?

how: hal (yes/no question word) + tuHibb (you like, to a man) + al-khubz (the bread)
notes: Here the l of al- is said clearly (al-khubz), unlike ad-dajaaj, where it blends into the d.
To a woman: hal tuHibbiin al-khubz?

how: hal (yes/no question word) + tuHibbiin (you like, to a woman) + al-khubz (the bread)
notes: To a man: hal tuHibb al-khubz?

how: laa (not) + uHibb (I like) + al-khubz (the bread)
notes: Arabic says 'the bread' for bread in general.

how: khubz (bread) + wa (and) + dajaaj (chicken)
notes: wa is written joined to the next word.

how: hal (yes/no question word) + cindaka (you have, to a man) + akh (brother)
notes: Answer with a full sentence: cindii akh, ismuhu [name], or laysa cindii akh.
To a woman: hal cindaki akh?

how: hal (yes/no question word) + cindaki (you have, to a woman) + ukht (sister)
notes: Don't mix them up: ukht (sister) has u at the start and t at the end; akh (brother) has neither.
To a man: hal cindaka ukht?

how: cindii (I have) + akh (brother): literally 'at me, a brother'.
notes: For a full answer, add his name: cindii akh, ismuhu [name] ('his name is').

how: laysa (not) + cindii (I have) + ukht (sister)
notes: laysa, not laa: cindii isn't a verb.

how: laysa (not) + cindii (I have) + akh (brother)

notes: Borrowed from 'telephone': Arabic has no e or o vowels, so it comes out tilifuun.

how: raqm (number) + tilifuun (phone) + -ak (your, to a man)
notes: 'In Arabic we flip them': raqm (number) comes first, then tilifuun (phone).
To a woman: raqm tilifuunik.
Levantine: nimrit tilifuunak.

how: maa (what) + raqm tilifuunak (your phone number)
notes: She accepts maa or maadhaa; the book uses maa before a noun (maa ismuka?), so maa is the safe choice.

how: laysa (not) + cindii (I have) + tilifuun (phone)
khubz (bread) + ciraaqii (Iraqi): the noun first, then the describing word.
notes: Boat-shaped and thick, one layer (not two).
Arabic names breads by country: khubz + the nationality word.
flag: translit caraaqii contradicts the kasra under the cayn (Iraq = al-ciraaq): fix to 'khubz ciraaqii'

how: al-ciraaq (Iraq) drops its al- and adds -ii ('from'): Iraqi.
notes: This -ii means 'from (a place)', not 'my'.
flag: translit caraaqii contradicts the kasra under the cayn (Iraq = al-ciraaq): fix to 'ciraaqii'

how: khubz (bread) + suurii (Syrian): the noun first, then the describing word.
notes: Flat, with two layers.
Arabic names breads by country: khubz + the nationality word.

how: Country + -ii ('from'): Syria becomes suurii, like lubnaan (Lebanon) becomes lubnaanii.
notes: This -ii means 'from (a place)', not 'my'.
For a woman: suuriyya.

how: khubz (bread) + lubnaanii (Lebanese: lubnaan + -ii, 'from')
notes: The thinnest: two very thin layers.

how: khubz (bread) + baagiit, the French word 'baguette'
notes: She said they just call it by its French name.
Arabic has no g letter, so borrowed words often write the g sound with ghayn.
